To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the existence of multiple balanced states in recurrent networks depends on the relative size of the local recurrent excitability and inhibition, and that fluctuation-driven balanced activity in the simplest models of this type is not robust, and is unlikely to occur in realistic networks.

In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the existence of a bistable balance condition with two coexisting stable steady states, one with subthreshold mean drive and low firing rate and the other with suprathreshold mean drive and high firing rate, is not a robust prediction of the simplified models considered in this paper.

the coexistence of multiple balanced states is possible, but the precise balance condition is very sensitive to the network parameters, and therefore the phenomenon might be difficult to observe in real networks.
the coexistence of two balanced steady states in a network model of cortical neurons is a possibility, but not a robust property.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the existence of a fluctuation-driven persistent state is not ruled out by the present study, but its robustness is not guaranteed.
the coexistence of two balanced states, one with low firing rate and one with high firing rate, is a possible scenario for the network dynamics in the delay period of persistent activity tasks.

, while balanced steady states of recurrent networks of current-driven LIF neurons are possible, the degree of balance is not sufficient to explain the observed high degree of irregular spiking during persistent activity in the delay period of a working memory task.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the existence of a fluctuation-driven persistent state requires the fine-tuning of a number of parameters, and that this fine-tuning increases for larger network sizes.
the coexistence of different stable states of the same network can be used to explain how the same network supports both the low firing rate states and the persistent states of working memory.

, in the context of the mean field theory of recurrent networks, the coexistence of two balanced steady states with different firing rates is not an inevitable consequence of the balance condition, but rather a delicate and fragile feature that is not robust against model simplifications.
